title: The TCP Maximum Segment Size and Related Topics
summary: This RFC clarifies the TCP Maximum Segment Size option and how it interacts with IP, offering advice to implementers. It explains what the option means and why getting it wrong causes trouble. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo settles what the TCP Maximum Segment Size option means. It fixes one rule: the maximum segment size is the largest IP datagram the path allows, minus the 40 bytes of a minimal IP and TCP header. The default is 536 bytes of data per segment.

subtitle: The memo that pins down what the TCP Maximum Segment Size option counts: the IP datagram size minus forty.

tldr.problem: The TCP specification defined the Maximum Segment Size option ambiguously, and both the IP and TCP headers can vary in length, so implementers disagreed about what the number in the option referred to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states one rule: the TCP Maximum Segment Size is the IP maximum datagram size minus forty. The default IP maximum datagram size is 576 octets, so the default MSS is 536 octets, and the option counts data octets only.
tldr.outcome: RFC 879 is Historic. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293 and updated by RFC 6691, which carry the same rule forward.

facts.label: What MSS counts
facts.value: Data octets only, not the TCP or IP header

today: RFC 879 is Historic. Its rule survives in RFC 9293, the consolidated TCP specification, and the memo itself was obsoleted by RFC 7805 and RFC 9293 and updated by RFC 6691.

sections.title: Why the Option Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
RFC 879 discusses the TCP Maximum Segment Size option and its relation to the IP Maximum Datagram Size, and it says plainly that it exists because the current specification of the option is ambiguous. Much of the difficulty in understanding the two sizes comes from the variable length of the IP and TCP headers.

The memo opens by restating a long-established rule: hosts must not send datagrams larger than 576 octets unless they have specific knowledge that the destination host is prepared to accept larger datagrams.

To remove the ambiguity, the memo establishes a single rule: the TCP Maximum Segment Size is the IP Maximum Datagram Size minus forty. The default IP Maximum Datagram Size is 576, so the default TCP Maximum Segment Size is 536.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP lets each side say the biggest chunk of data it wants to receive. The rule here is simple: that number is the IP datagram size minus 40, which leaves room for the two headers.

sections.title: The Maximum Segment Size Option
sections.content:
TCP provides an option that may be used at the time a connection is established, and only at that time, to indicate the maximum size of TCP segment that can be accepted on that connection. The announcement is sent from the data receiver to the data sender and says "I can accept TCP segments up to size X". The memo notes that this announcement is often mistakenly called a negotiation.

The value X may be larger or smaller than the default, and the MSS can be used completely independently in each direction of data flow, so the two directions of one connection may end up with quite different maximum sizes.

The MSS counts only data octets in the segment. It does not count the TCP header or the IP header. As a footnote the memo adds that the value also does not count the SYN and FIN control bits, even though those do consume TCP sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side of a connection states once, at connection setup, the largest segment it can accept. The number covers payload bytes only, so headers do not eat into it.

sections.title: Relating Segment Size to Datagram Size
sections.content:
The memo gives the calculation for the MSS value to send, and then for the segment size that can be sent after receiving one:

MSS = MTU - sizeof(TCPHDR) - sizeof(IPHDR)

SndMaxSegSiz = MIN((MTU - sizeof(TCPHDR) - sizeof(IPHDR)), MSS)

The open question is which values to use for the two header sizes. The memo presents three reasonable positions. The conservative position assumes both headers are at their maximum, 60 octets each, giving MSS = MTU - 120, which is 456 when the MTU is 576. The moderate position assumes a maximum IP header of 60 octets and a minimum TCP header of 20 octets, giving MSS = MTU - 80, which is 496. The liberal position assumes both headers are at their minimum of 20 octets, giving MSS = MTU - 40, which is 536.

The memo argues for the liberal position on practical grounds: minimum headers are the common case, so limiting the segment data to less than could be transmitted at once wastes capacity, especially below 512 octets. For comparison it gives the data share of a 576-octet datagram: 536 is 93 percent, 496 is 86 percent, and 456 is 79 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: To turn a link's packet size into a segment size, subtract the headers. The memo argues for subtracting the smallest possible headers, because headers are usually short and the leftover space can carry real data.

sections.title: Source and Gateway Fragmentation
sections.content:
A source host would not normally create datagram fragments. Under normal circumstances fragments only arise when a gateway must send a datagram into a network with a smaller maximum packet size. The gateway must then fragment the datagram, unless it is marked "don't fragment", in which case it is discarded, with the option of sending an ICMP message to the source reporting the problem.

It might be desirable for the source host to send datagrams itself in fragments if the maximum segment size allowed by the receiver were larger than the maximum packet size of the directly attached network, but such fragments must not combine to a size larger than the destination host allows.

Gateways must be prepared to fragment; it is not an optional feature. They have no information about the size of datagrams destination hosts are prepared to accept, and it would be inappropriate for gateways to try to keep such information. They must accept the largest datagrams allowed on each directly attached network, even if larger than 576 octets, and must fragment datagrams to fit the next network even if that is smaller than 576 octets.

The memo outlaws a particular source behaviour: a source that sends a datagram larger than the default size on the assumption that the gateway will fragment it into default-sized fragments. If the destination host cannot accept datagrams larger than the default, it probably cannot reassemble them either, so the mail will not arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: When a packet is too big for the next link, a router splits it into smaller pieces and the receiver puts it back together. The memo says routers must do this, but senders must not push large packets at routers and hope.

sections.title: How the Layers Pass Sizes to Each Other
sections.content:
The memo is explicit that there must be communication between protocol layers and program modules, but that it should be carefully specified and controlled. It observes that IP is a one-shot datagram protocol with no memory of transmitted datagrams, so it is not appropriate for IP to keep information about the maximum datagram size a particular destination host might accept, while TCP is an end-to-end reliable stream protocol that does remember many things about the state of a connection.

The described chain is short. The network driver or interface knows the maximum transmission unit of the directly attached network. IP asks the driver for that value. TCP asks IP for the Maximum Datagram Data Size, defined as the MTU minus the IP header length. When opening a connection, TCP can send an MSS option with the value equal to the Maximum Datagram Data Size minus the TCP header length. TCP then determines the Maximum Segment Data Size from either the default or the received option, and determines whether source fragmentation is possible and desirable by asking IP. IP checks the length of the data passed to it by TCP: if the length is at or below the Maximum Datagram Data Size, IP attaches the IP header and hands it to the network driver; otherwise IP must do source fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer asks the one below it for the limit it works with. The driver knows the link size, IP subtracts its header, and TCP subtracts its own.
